BBC News, 16 November 2026

UK lost more than it gained from Brexit, Burnham to say ahead of EU summit

Andy Burnham touches his chin as he sits in front of the UK and EU flags while attending a business summit at the Chancellery in Berlin in October.

The prime minister is expected to argue that the UK has lost more than it has gained from leaving the European Union in a speech ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels later this week.

Speaking at the Lord Mayor's Banquet on Monday, Andy Burnham will compare the UK's Brexit deal to the \"emperor's new clothes\" - saying \"a needlessly hard Brexit\" created barriers for businesses and the promise to \"take back control\" was not delivered.

He is seeking to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility with the bloc at Friday's summit, where he has said a \"win-win\" deal can be struck.

The Conservatives have said Labour are \"dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset\".

Burnham is expected to say on Monday: \"It's like the emperor's new clothes – where no-one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on.

\"The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we have gained.\"

The prime minister says he wants to reset Britain's relationship with the EU - and his argument is not that Brexit was wrong, but the way it happened was.

He will say any deal must pass the \"Makerfield test\" of providing tangible improvements to everyday lives, and deliver an arrangement which is closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.

Burnham is also expected to restate his commitment to Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledge that there would be \"no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement\".

He will say the prospect of a new deal is a \"win-win\" and illustrates a \"new approach\".

\"Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges. But being constructive and positive - showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges.\"

Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election, although he has also made clear he wants to examine the \"pros and cons\" of the options for Britain's long-term relationship with the bloc.

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer struck a deal in May 2025 covering fishing, trade and other areas, and this week's summit will see the UK government seek to agree further changes.

The UK and EU agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports ahead of the meeting.

Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated to EU nations.

Deputy Conservative leader Alex Burghart said that \"instead of tackling the spiralling welfare bill, fixing our economy, and properly funding our defence, Burnham is preparing to hand Brussels more money in an effort to distract from the mess his party has gotten us into\".

The Liberal Democrats said earlier this month that the draft deal on food exports was a \"patch, not a fix\" and that the \"real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU\".

Reform UK has said one of the \"key benefits\" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to \"adhere to ridiculous EU rules\", and argued that any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy.

The Green Party of England and Wales has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying \"full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK\".
